summary: Defines MADCAP, a protocol that lets hosts request multicast addresses from multicast address allocation servers. It is a standards-track document at the proposed standard level.

eli5.summary: It is like asking a clerk for a free channel number for your group chat so nobody else picks the same one.

questions: how do hosts get multicast addresses
how does madcap differ from dhcp
what is a madcap lease identifier
subtitle: How a host asks a server for a multicast address, borrows it for a while, and hands it back.

tldr.problem: Multicast applications need group addresses that nobody else is using at the same time, and the multicast address space is fairly small. Hosts need a standard way to get one quickly without extra network load.
tldr.mechanism: MADCAP is a client-server protocol over UDP. A client sends DISCOVER, REQUEST, RENEW, RELEASE or GETINFO messages, and servers answer with OFFER, ACK or NAK, so each address is handed out as a time-limited lease.
tldr.outcome: MADCAP gives hosts a policy-neutral way to lease multicast addresses, renew or release them, and learn which multicast scopes exist. It has only basic built-in security and recommends IPsec when security matters.

today: RFC 2730 is a Proposed Standard from December 1999. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the published specification of MADCAP.

sections.title: What MADCAP Is For
sections.content:
The Multicast Address Dynamic Client Allocation Protocol (MADCAP) lets hosts request multicast address allocation services from multicast address allocation servers. It is one part of the Multicast Address Allocation Architecture being defined by the IETF Multicast Address Allocation Working Group, but it may be used separately from the rest of that architecture.

The RFC lists what such a protocol needs: a quick response, low network load for hosts that are not allocating anything, support for intermittently connected or power managed systems, both administratively scoped and globally scoped addresses, efficient use of a scarce address space, authentication to guard against hoarding, neutrality about allocation policy, and support for conferences where members can modify a lease.

MADCAP was originally based on DHCP and shares some similarities, so code might be shared. It is still completely separate from DHCP, with no dependencies between the two.
sections.eli5: When many groups want to talk at once, each needs its own address so conversations do not get mixed up. MADCAP is the sign-up desk that hands them out fairly.

sections.title: Scopes, Leases and Lease Identifiers
sections.content:
A multicast scope is a range of multicast addresses configured so that traffic sent to them stays within part of the internetwork. One scope can have several instances, called scope zones. A Scope ID is the lowest numbered address in a scope. Clients must say which scope they want addresses from, and servers can supply a Multicast Scope List with the address range, a maximum TTL or hop count, and one or more human-readable zone names for each zone.

Every MADCAP message carries a Lease Identifier option. It must be unique across all leases requested by all clients in a multicast address allocation domain. Type 0 is a Random Lease Identifier (at least 16 octets from a decent random number generator is recommended). Type 1 is an Address-Specific Lease Identifier, built from an address family number, an address and a client-specific identifier. Servers should treat the identifier as opaque, and use it to match RENEW and RELEASE messages to the original lease.

If a client cannot learn its scope list, it may temporarily assume a single scope: for IPv4, the IPv4 Local Scope (239.255.0.0/16) with a maximum TTL of 16, and for IPv6, SCOP 3 with a maximum hop count of 16.
sections.eli5: A scope is how far your announcement is allowed to travel, like a school, a town or the whole world. The lease number is your ticket stub that proves the address is yours for now.

sections.title: Message Format and Options
sections.content:
All MADCAP messages are UDP datagrams. The server uses port 2535, assigned by IANA, and clients may use any port. The fixed part has four fields: version (1 octet, zero for this specification), msgtype (1 octet), addrfamily (2 octets) and xid (4 octets), followed by variable-length options. A message too short to hold this format (at least 12 bytes) MUST be ignored, as must a message with a nonzero version.

Each option has a two octet code, a two octet length and then the value. The options field MUST end with the End option (code 0), and a message MUST NOT contain two options of the same type. Unrecognized options are ignored, while a message that breaks the rules makes a server generate an Invalid Request error and makes a client ignore the message. Options defined include Lease Time (1), Server Identifier (2), Lease Identifier (3), Multicast Scope (4), Option Request List (5), Start Time (6), Number of Addresses Requested (7), Requested Language (8), Multicast Scope List (9), List of Address Ranges (10), Current Time (11), Feature List (12), Retry Time (13), Minimum Lease Time (14), Maximum Start Time (15) and Error (16).

Times are 32-bit unsigned seconds since 00:00 UTC, 1st January 1970. A table in the RFC says which options MUST, MAY or MUST NOT appear in each message type.
sections.eli5: Every MADCAP note starts with a small fixed form (what kind of note, which conversation) and then a list of labeled extras, with a special END marker at the bottom.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Talk
sections.content:
Eight message types exist. Clients send DISCOVER, REQUEST, RENEW, RELEASE and GETINFO. Servers send OFFER, ACK and NAK. REQUEST, RENEW and RELEASE are unicast to a server, which answers with an ACK or NAK. GETINFO asks for information such as the scope list, or finds servers, and can be multicast to a MADCAP Server Multicast Address: the address IANA reserved at a relative offset of -1 from the last address of a scope.

DISCOVER is always multicast. Servers that can probably satisfy the request temporarily reserve addresses and unicast an OFFER. The client picks a server and multicasts a REQUEST containing that server's Server Identifier to the same address, so the other servers can stop holding their reservations. The chosen server replies with an ACK or NAK. A server SHOULD hold offered addresses for [OFFER-HOLD], recommended to be at least 60 seconds. A server MUST NOT offer a lease shorter than the client's minimum lease time or a start time later than the client's maximum.

Retransmission is the client's job. The recommended scheme is a 4 second delay before the first retransmission, doubling each time up to 16 seconds, with at most three retransmissions (at t+4, t+12 and t+28). The xid, message type and Lease Identifier together must be probably unique over [XID-REUSE-INTERVAL], 10 minutes. Servers cache responses, recommended for sixty seconds and at most 300 seconds, and resend the cached reply to a retransmitted request, because requests are not idempotent.
sections.eli5: You shout "who has a free number?", helpers each hold one for you, you pick one helper, and the others let theirs go. If nobody answers, you wait a bit longer each time before asking again.

sections.title: Optional Features, Clock Skew and Errors
sections.content:
Optional features have two-octet codes and are negotiated with the Feature List option, which has supported, requested and required lists. Three are defined: Server Mobility (0) lets a lease allocated on one server be renewed or released on another; Retry After (1) lets a server ask the client to come back later for large or slow allocations, using the Retry Time option; and Shared Lease Identifier (2) lets any client that knows the Lease Identifier modify a lease, which helps conferences.

Multicast sessions are often advertised with absolute times, so a client with a wrong clock could cause two sessions to share an address. The Current Time option lets the receiver detect clock skew. Servers should allocate an extra period, [EXTRA-ALLOCATION-TIME] (recommended default one hour), on either side of a lease. If skew exceeds [CLOCK-SKEW-ALLOWANCE] (recommended default 30 minutes) the server MUST generate an Excessive Clock Skew error.

A NAK carries an Error option. Defined codes are 0 (valid request could not be completed), 1 (invalid request), 2 (excessive clock skew), 3 (Lease Identifier not recognized) and 4 (required feature not supported). Codes 1024-2047 are reserved for experimental use. Servers should not answer a NAK or an unclear message with another NAK, to avoid NAK loops.
sections.eli5: Some extras are optional, like letting a friend change your booking. Also, if your watch is an hour wrong, the clerk gives you some extra time around your booking so two groups do not collide.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls MADCAP's security requirements relatively basic. The multicast routing and management protocols cannot currently enforce authorized use of a multicast address, so an allocation only means that no one else will (most likely) be given that address for the lease period. It does not restrict who may send to it.

Clients may want to authenticate servers to avoid rogue ones, and servers may want to authenticate clients for auditing or to limit how many addresses one client takes. Data integrity is a strong requirement, while confidentiality is not, except when the Shared Lease Identifier feature is used. In that case the Lease Identifier must be kept confidential by encrypting messages and using a cryptographically random identifier of at least eight octets.

When security is a strong requirement, IPsec SHOULD protect all unicast MADCAP messages, and with IPsec in use the server MUST drop all multicast packets except GETINFO.
sections.eli5: The clerk can only promise that nobody else will be given your number. It cannot stop someone from shouting on it, so for important things you add a lock using IPsec.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC defines five number spaces: MADCAP options, message types, Lease Identifier types, features and error codes. Certain values are defined in the specification, and new values may only be defined by IETF Consensus, which basically means by RFCs approved by the IESG.

Appendix B lists recommended values for the protocol's constants, such as [XID-REUSE-INTERVAL] at 10 minutes (required), [NO-RESPONSE-DELAY] at 60 seconds and [RESPONSE-CACHE-INTERVAL] at least 60 seconds with a 5 minute maximum.
sections.eli5: The numbers for message kinds and options are kept in an official list, and adding a new one needs the IETF's agreement.

fields.name: version
fields.desc: Protocol version, zero for this specification.

fields.name: msgtype
fields.desc: Message type such as DISCOVER or GETINFO.

fields.desc: Default address family for the message.

fields.name: xid
fields.desc: Transaction identifier chosen by the client.

items.label: DISCOVER
items.desc: Client multicast to find servers that can probably satisfy a REQUEST.

items.label: OFFER
items.desc: Server unicast reply to DISCOVER, holding addresses.

items.label: RENEW
items.desc: Client changes the lease time or start time of an existing lease.

items.label: ACK
items.desc: Server answers GETINFO, REQUEST, RENEW or RELEASE affirmatively.

items.label: NAK
items.desc: Server answers negatively and includes an Error option.

items.label: RELEASE
items.desc: Client gives up a lease before it expires.

items.label: GETINFO
items.desc: Client asks for information such as the scope list.

messages.label: DISCOVER
messages.note: Multicast to a MADCAP Server Multicast Address.

messages.label: OFFER
messages.note: Unicast; each willing server holds addresses.

items.label: Valid Request Could Not Be Completed
items.desc: Request valid but cannot be met with available addresses and configuration.

items.label: Invalid Request
items.desc: Request malformed or invalid in some other way.

items.label: Excessive Clock Skew
items.desc: Client and server clocks differ too much.

items.label: Lease Identifier Not Recognized
items.desc: Usually in response to RENEW or RELEASE.

items.label: Required Feature Not Supported
items.desc: A feature in the required list is not supported.
